title: Between two opinions (1 Kings 18:21–39)
hook: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" on Mount Carmel

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow in Zarephath shared her last handful of flour, and the jar, her kad, didn't fail. Did you share from the little you had? Today Elijah leaves the widow's house and climbs a mountain to face a whole people. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

Mount Carmel, and the slope is full of people. King Ahab has sent for all the children of Israel, and they've come up to watch a contest. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god Queen Jezebel favors. On the other side stands one man: Elijah. The land has had no rain for a long time. Before any fire is lit, before any altar is built, Elijah turns, not to the king and not to the prophets, but to the people watching. And he asks them a question.
screen: `ALL ISRAEL ON MOUNT CARMEL.` → `ONE MAN AND A CROWD.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the question, in the King James words: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" To halt, in old English, is to limp. It's the image of someone hobbling, one foot on each side of a fork in the road, never quite walking down either. Then Elijah finishes the thought: if the Lord be God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him. And then the text gives the crowd's reply. The people answered him not a word. Silence. Nobody wants to choose. What follows is the contest. Two altars, two bulls, no fire. Whoever answers with fire is God. The prophets of Baal call out from morning until noon, and the text says, there was no voice, nor any that answered. Elijah rebuilds a broken altar of the Lord, has water poured over it until the trench runs full, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls and consumes everything, even the water in the trench. And now the people, who said not a word before, fall on their faces and say: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." Remember that the question came before the fire. Elijah was after an end to the limping. In Jewish practice, the people's cry from this chapter returns at the very end of Yom Kippur, called out by the whole congregation as the gates of the day close. A people that once could not answer at all now answers together. The story keeps the uncomfortable middle part, too: the long silence, the people waiting to see who would win before they spoke. It doesn't pretend that choosing is easy. It only asks how long.
screen: `HOW LONG HALT YE?` · `THE PEOPLE ANSWERED NOT A WORD.` · then, large: `FIRE ON THE REBUILT ALTAR.` · then: `THE LORD, HE IS THE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one thing you've wavered on. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind something you've been limping on, one foot on each side: a call you keep almost making, a habit you keep almost dropping, a yes or a no you've left hanging. Small is fine. Notice what the waiting has cost: the energy of standing at the fork. Then, quietly, pick one side. You don't have to act on it this minute. Just let the decision land, the way the people's silence finally turned into words. If you pray, you can ask for clarity. The bell holds the time.
Halt. The old word for limping, what Elijah said the people were doing between two opinions. Today's word.
Your line: how long between two opinions. Today, when you catch yourself hovering over a choice, ask it plainly, how long, and then take one step. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read the contest on Mount Carmel as a haftarah, and at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out the people's words from this chapter, that the Lord is God.

fork.setup: you're in the crowd on Mount Carmel. Elijah asks how long you will limp between two opinions. what does the crowd do?
options: shout out for the Lord at once.
fork.reveal: the people answered him not a word. only after the fire falls do they cry out, the Lord, he is the God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fire-from-heaven contest.
what it means: Elijah wants a wavering people to stop limping and choose.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew verb for limping returns in verse 26, where Baal's prophets limp around their altar.

notes: Auditor (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced rough cloak; softened the narrator's verdict on Elijah's motive; trapdoor scholar floor now gives the Hebrew detail (the limping root of 18:21 returns at 18:26, JPS "danced in halting wise"). KJV is used for 18:21/18:39 on a JPS path; JPS 1917 18:39 reads "The LORD, He is God", Keeper may switch.

Editor: removed the hook's repeated 'slope' and the unsupported line that everyone was tired and frightened; replaced 'Picture someone hobbling' with a non-template phrasing; cut 'famous' (unsourced).
Quotes use KJV (1769); JPS 1917 is close at 18:21 but a Keeper may prefer the JPS wording throughout.
'there was no voice, nor any that answered' (18:26) and 'answered him not a word' (18:21) are given without quotation marks as near-KJV; verify or keep as paraphrase.

howItsDone: confirm the Carmel chapter is read as a haftarah (Ki Tisa, by most customs) and the Neilah close of Yom Kippur with the congregational Adonai hu ha-Elohim. No count of repetitions is stated on purpose.
'Halt' as old English for 'limp' is standard KJV usage; Keeper may wish to add the Hebrew posechim.
